analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay frontline health workers 25% extra during federal health emergencies, reimbursed through a payroll tax credit.
analysis.headline: Introduced during the first COVID-19 surge with 11 cosponsors, the bill was referred to two committees the same day, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During any federally declared public health emergency, employers would have to pay covered health care workers at least 25% above their regular rate. The federal government would reimburse employers for the entire cost through a refundable payroll tax credit, and Social Security trust funds would be made whole for lost payroll revenue. The bill never got past its first day: it was sent to two committees and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: Frontline health care employees — workers in the Bureau of Labor Statistics practitioner and support groups, such as nurses, physicians, EMTs, nursing assistants, and home health aides — would earn 125% of their regular pay for the duration of any federal public health emergency. Dentists, physical therapists, and a list of other excluded occupations would not qualify. Enforcing the pay would work like a minimum-wage claim under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to pay covered health care employees at least 125% of their regular rate during a federal public-health emergency period.

Covers direct-care occupations in BLS major groups 29 and 31 — including nurses, physicians, EMTs, nursing assistants, and home health aides — while excluding dentists, optometrists, physical therapists, and similar occupations.
Enforcement is treated as a violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act's minimum-wage provisions, giving workers an established legal route to recover unpaid hazard pay.
Employers get a refundable tax credit equal to 100% of the hazard wages paid each quarter, so even employers whose payroll taxes fall short of the credit receive the difference back as a refund.
The bill transfers general-fund money to the Social Security trust funds to replace payroll tax revenue lost to the credit, so the hazard pay mandate does not drain Social Security.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. Because the credit covers 100% of the hazard wages and is fully refundable, the entire cost of the pay premium during an emergency would fall on the Treasury, not on employers or on the Social Security trust funds.

drawbacks.text: The cost to the Treasury is open-ended: the credit is fully refundable and uncapped, so during a long national emergency the federal government would reimburse every covered employer's entire 25% premium.
Employers must pay the premium up front and wait for a quarterly credit, creating a cash-flow burden for thinly capitalized providers such as small home care agencies.

Coverage has gaps: the bill excludes many frontline occupations — dental assistants, pharmacy aides, medical records technicians, therapy aides — and covers only health care workers, leaving out grocery, transit, and other essential workers facing the same exposure.
Compliance depends on workers enforcing their own rights through Fair Labor Standards Act claims, which historically under-deters violations in low-wage care work.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is honest: workers get a real 25% premium, employers are made whole, and Social Security is not raided to pay for it. The genuine costs are the uncapped federal outlay during a prolonged emergency and the narrow scope — it protects only one slice of the essential workforce and omits several lower-paid care occupations. It would have been a targeted, fully financed benefit rather than an unfunded mandate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or floor time before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on April 10, 2020, during the first COVID-19 surge, with Rep. Kendra S. Horn as the other original sponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Labor Committee, which cover the tax credit and the wage mandate respectively.
Eleven House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no further action of any kind followed.
Neither committee held a hearing or markup, the bill never reached the House floor, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care employers faced no mandated 25% wage premium during the pandemic, and the Treasury avoided an open-ended reimbursement obligation. Covered frontline health workers never received the hazard pay.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers; frontline workers got nothing

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors were Democrats and no Republican took a recorded position, but the bill never came to a vote, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill would have required hospitals to pay a 25% wage premium up front during emergencies, but a fully refundable tax credit would have reimbursed 100% of it, leaving only cash-flow and record-keeping burdens. Hospital employers had an interest in not having the mandate at all, while their workers would have gained the premium.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and home health agencies
industries.note: These employers rely heavily on the lower-paid support occupations in BLS group 31 that the bill covers, so the 25% premium would have raised their payrolls during emergencies — with the same full reimbursement through the refundable credit. Up-front payment before the quarterly credit would still have strained cash flow.
